then start having a little bit more fun or at least for me I find this phase particularly fun and you can go through and do different specific passes to improve your story so I like to do a character pass you know where I'm literally just focusing on characters sometimes I'll literally just focus on like one character I might go through and say I'm just going to focus on the mentor character here just going to try to make them really inspiring trying to make them very motivating for my main

character and I'm just going to go through from start to finish focusing on them that might be a couple of days worth of writing it might be a few weeks worth of writing and editing but it's a really fun exercise to do because you're not worried about all the other things going on in your story you're just looking at this one specific element and trying to make it as good as you possibly can the other pass you might want to look at here is a dialogue pass just go through only focus on the

dialogue and see how you can improve that make it more distinctive for every character probably the biggest hack here and I'll let you in on a little secret when it comes to dialogue I've pretty much never met a bit of dialogue that hasn't been improved by just condensing it I find that in almost every case with my writing shortening the dialogue compressing it down to its Essentials always makes it better the other thing you can look at is a hook pass so this is something I like to look at at the

start and finish of each chapter basically just making sure that I'm always re hooking readers at the start of each chapter in an interesting way and I'm leading out of chapters in an interesting way as well you might want to look at a foreshadowing pass so if there's a big twist or some kind of mystery that's paid off at the end of your story you want to go back earlier on into the the book and figure out ways to sew the seeds to sew little clues of that so that it pays off in a good way

later on you may also like to do a setting pass for me personally I find that when I'm writing my first draft I can be pretty threadbear on my descriptions of places and I can write a lot of scenes where it's just characters talking in a bit of a white room so I like to have a specific setting pass where I go back through and I ask myself you know am I sort of incorporating the weather in here in an interesting way like if it's a noticeable season like if it's winter right now am I mentioning

the snow if it's summer am I mentioning the heat the blue skies all this sort of stuff and am I also setting each in the story in the most interesting location it can possibly be in a good example of this comes pretty early on in Kingdom of Dragons after Ren and Zora get to alium the floating Dragon Rider Academy they have this jeweling sequence where they're jeweling against some of the other Cadets up there and originally it just sort of took place in a generic room but I decided to set it someplace a

bit more interesting I thought wouldn't it be cool if they're having this practice Jewel in a room that's sort of in the caverns of alium and they're on this sort of rocky bridge above a shallow pool of water so you know if you get knocked off the bridge then you fall into the water and maybe one of my characters in this case you know Zora this girl over here maybe she actually manipulates that in a way to win a jewel that she wouldn't otherwise and so it's just a little tweak but it makes the

scene so much more interesting by just adding in this extra layer and of course you can add in any other the passes that are appropriate for you as well as you develop as a writer you're going to figure out what things you typically need to work on in your edit because you're maybe you know not as good as expressing that in the first first draft again this is the beauty of writing like you don't have to do everything at once and in fact just focusing on these different passes and knowing like this

week I'm just going to work on my dialogue next week I'm just going to work on my setting it is so deliberating and it actually to me is probably like the funnest part of the writing process in a lot of ways I really do enjoy outlining as well but this is just so fun cuz you kind of know that the basic story is there and now you're just getting to tweak and play with things so at this stage your story will probably be ready to give to early readers you don't don't necessarily want your story

to be perfect before you give to early readers because if you've invested too much time too much effort into the editing then you give it to early readers you might be more resistant to the advice they give you you want to kind of find that sweet spot where like the bones of the story are there but there's still a lot of room for improvement and you know that there's going to be more Improvement to come because that's going to allow you to have the sort of mental fortitude and creative energy to incorporate their

feedback and you know actually continue improving your story so this phase of the process is about finding people who can give you honest feedback again the fantasy Writers Guild my community for Fantasy writers is something that can help you with this we've got a whole feedback system set up in there we've even got a feedback matcher who you can basically message them and they will pair you up with another writer who also wants to give feedback so that you can you know swap your chapters with each

other and really learn from both the process of giving a critique and receiving a critique at the same time because it's very very useful to give feedback to other writers too and the main thing to be focusing on with your early readers is to be asking for their experience and their emotions this is really really critical and it's why I've bolded it here because you don't necessarily want to ask for their advice and for their Direction let me clarify what I mean here the reason for this is

because most early readers you work with you know whether they are family and friends or colleagues or you know even other writers they probably haven't been trained as a Specialized or professional editor and so sometimes they are going to be well actually let me say that again if they describe their emotional experience of your story and they're like you know I really connected with this character because of this or you know I didn't quite find this scene worked for me they are 100% right you

cannot argue with their actual emotional experience of what the story has done to them however if they turn around and they're like I think you should do this to fix it they might not always be accurate because they might lack the full understanding about what you're trying to achieve or they might not actually have the skill to know how to come in and diagnose and edit a story so you do want to be cautious when you are working with early readers if they don't actually have extensive editorial

experience or that you know haven't been trained in proper editing because they may lack the ability to give you a correct solution to the problem it is much more useful to just gauge their experience their emotion their reaction to the story and use that as Clues to then come up with a solution on your own as a writer obviously you know if you're working with a professional editor or someone who is a really good writer then you can probably ask for more prescriptive advice from them but

generally speaking you want to focus on their experience and their emotions the four questions I like to use to do this first of all what's great about the story so that I don't accidentally get rid of it what's boring so that I do get rid of it or change it what confuses you you know what didn't really make sense here and then lastly what don't you believe so was there a character decision that felt very unusual or was there something about the world that just didn't have the logic working

properly I got these four questions from Mary robinet Cowell and these are pretty much the questions you know I'll be sending through to my early readers Whenever I send them a story so you know the early readers for Kingdom of Dragons these were the questions I was getting them to answer the important thing here is you really want your early readers to focus on Big Picture notes you don't necessarily want them to be coming in and be correcting spelling or grammar or punctuation because all of these things

are probably going to change later on and that's not really the focus of what an early reader critique should be about it should be about the big picture structure of your story so for example right here we've got an email I sent to one of my early readers for Kingdom of Dragons Maddie who you know gave me some amazing feedback on this book a few years ago and you can see here these are the questions that I sent through to her I said you know this is an early draft so there's going to be a lot of typos

don't worry about correcting them I'll fix them in the proof reading stages what I want is Big piture of feedback so you know what's awesome what's boring what's confusing what didn't you believe when it comes to receiving feedback oh boy this is this is a really tough thing to to go through as a writer it is going to hurt like even to this day you know like I've been writing for 12 years I've published a lot of books I've read a lot of reviews and everything it still

always hurts when an early reader tells you that something didn't quite work and the reality is that right now you're probably not as good as you think you are I know it's a bit of a harsh thing to say but if you have not like published multiple books yet or you know you haven't finished a book yet you probably don't know the deficiencies that are in your kind of skills as a writer and that is totally okay because every single person starts there your favorite author they start there in the

exact same spot so don't take negative feedback personally in fact really detach yourself from the idea that there is negative and positive feedback there's just feedback right that's all there is and your job is just to learn from it to develop a thick skin and to not let it harm your ego but to just use it as fuel to improve your story you and your readers your early readers you're both working together you're not on opposite teams you're not arguing or jeweling with them you're both working

together to form the best possible version of this story so treat your story as an experiment you know you're thinking that if I do these particular things in this scene it's going to make the reader feel this particular way your early readers are a way to validate that hypothesis to test that experiment and if something doesn't work then it just means that you need to change the variables of the experiment that you're running it's also worth noting here that you get feedback from what your early

readers don't say so you know if your early readers get seem to get like 20% of the way into the story and then their notes sort of dry up from there and they maybe just send feedback on the first 20% and you get this from like three or four people it's probably a sign that there's something you're doing in that first 20% that's not quite right and so the absence of feedback on the rest of the story is actually data and again if you are looking for a you know great community of fantasy writers to give you

high quality feedback on your story I highly suggest that you check out the guild like I said before we've got a feedback system set up in there and everyone who comes in is personally handpicked by me as well so you you know that you're not just getting a bunch of random people giving you feedback on your writing you're actually getting feedback from fellow fantasy writers who are really dedicated and really passionate about the craft as you are as well so once you've got that feedback

from your early readers it is now time for the fourth draft which is where you actually incorporate that feedback realize that you do not have to accept 100% of the notes that your early readers are going to give you again like I said before you want to ask for their experience and their emotions not necessarily their advice on what specifically to do again if your early readers are like actually really experienced writers or really experienced editors then you can accept some of that stuff a bit more but if

it's just you know family and friends or newer writers then you really need to be coming up with your own Solutions what you want to be doing though is look for patterns so if one person has a problem with a particular scene and you've sent it out to five people and the other four people didn't really have a problem with it and you kind of like the scene then maybe you can leave it but if all five people say they hate that scene then you do need to do something to fix it so then once you've done that fourth draft

and you in operated that early reader feedback it might be time to think about hiring a pro editor now the amount of editing that you need to get for a book is going to depend on whether you're going down the traditional publication or the self-publication pathway but if you are self-publishing you know 100% you need to get an editor involved on your story even if you are going down the traditional route as well it is very worthwhile to get a good developmental editor on your book because you're just

going to learn so much from working with a pro who has you know edited dozens of stories before and actually has that experience to give you advice on what to do the thing with a pro editor here is that they're going to be able to solve problems with your story that your early readers can't ideally you want to find someone who has published similar books in your genre or at least has worked in similar books in your genre and think of this as a huge investment in your learning capabilities because the skills

and the kind of problem Solutions and the writing craft principles that you are going to learn from a good editor they don't just help you for this one book they're working on they're going to help you for every single book moving forward it's no good just writing a book and then not getting any editing done on it and not learning and just going off and writing 10 more books and still not learning because just doing the same thing 10 times doesn't actually make you grow what makes you grow is doing the

Thing Once learning from it failing knowing how to overcome that then taking those learnings into the next project doing the same thing there and eventually you just keep compounding your growth and your learnings as an author to the point where you then able to express stories in a magical way when it comes to editing there's a few different kind of types of editing that are available and it's important to know which one is best at this stage of the process we've got developmental editing

which looks at the big picture structure of your story we've got line editing which looks at the sort of Pros the style the sentence flow it's a little bit more micro oriented rather than developmental editing which is more macro and then you've got copy editing which is like grammar spelling punctuation what you might think of is more proof reading now I would highly suggest that you just focus on development editing to start with if you are self-publishing as well you probably want to copy edit in there as well but

developmental editing is going to be the most valuable for you at this phase in the process because it's going to allow you to just really understand whether the big picture aspects of your story are working properly it's also worthwhile saying that you know as someone who has done a lot of editing for other writers out there although my one-on-one editing program has been closed for the last year and a half because I've wanted to focus more on group coaching stuff on my videos and my

it can be pricey but is a worthwhile investment to be making into your growth as an author now this brings us to the final draft and of course you may have you know more or less numbers of drafts depends from Project to project but this last phase of the editing process is all about polishing so here I like to look at how I can sharpen my Pros to condense and cut the descriptions and the writing in my story sometimes I will like to actually change my font before I go through with this just as a way to again

needs something different from this and while your character might chase their want what they actually require is their need this leads to your character's truth so the truth is an antidote to the lie that helps the character progress and shift from their want to their need now by using these five core elements you can create one of the three types of character arcs the first Arc is a positive Arc where a character you know starts off with some kind of flaws they go on a experience they go on a journey

and it helps them overcome those flaws and become a better person the next type of Arc is a negative Arc where a character is maybe actually pretty good at the start but as the story continues their sort of moral foundations become eroded and they end up in a worse place than they were at the beginning then the Last Arc is a flat Arc so in a flat Arc the focus is less on how your character changes because your character is probably going to be pretty similar at the start of the story to how they are

at the end instead the focus is on how they interact with the world around them and how they interact with other characters who are maybe going through their own positive or negative arcs around them so when it comes to structuring a positive Arc your character is going to begin by initially fully believing the lie as a result of the ghost's influence on their life this means they're ignorant of the truth at the start of the story and so they're probably pursuing their want this external thing that they think will

Percy Jackson and the Lightning Thief follows a young 12-year-old boy who discovers he is the demigod son of Poseidon and that the Greek gods are alive and kicking in our modern world this first book in the series focuses on Percy and his friends Annabeth and Grover as they Quest Across America in an attempt to retrieve Zeus's stolen lightning bolt from Hades who they believe has taken this bolt in order to instigate a war between the gods one thing that's important to note right from the start is that you'll see here

I've got these rough percentage markers at the top you don't always need to be hitting the exact structural moment at the exact percentage mark that is just unrealistic in many cases however you will typically find that a lot of the points I'm going to discuss here will fall around these benchmarks but it's more about just moving through all of these nine points in order and using it as a rough guideline a rough scaffold that helps you build a structure when you're creating a house no one is

building the scaffold for the sake of building the scaffold they're using the scaffold as a way to actually construct that second story as a way to fix the roof or to get the tiles up there that is the same approach you want to have so the first point is the hook so the hook is where you introduce your main character and especially their flaws desires key traits you know personality perspective all of that sort of stuff that makes them feel unique in a compelling way you ideally want to show

a somewhat characteristic moment here a moment that immediately explains to the reader what makes this person different what makes them special what makes them interesting to follow in the rest of the story so in in the case of Percy Jackson our opening Hook is we meet Percy who is a troubled 12-year-old kid he has 80hd and dyslexia and he feels like a huge Outsider he only really has one other friend this guy called Grover who also seems a bit like an outsider a bit of a misfit as well and on a school trip to a

Ordinary World of your character's lives is disrupted by a key event that sets the story in motion so in the case of Percy Jackson while camping on a trip with his mother Percy's friend Grover appears and Grover basically says he's being chased by this monster called The Minotaur so this you know horned big bull combined with a man from Greek mythology and Percy's mother basically realizes that she needs to drive him to this place called Camp Half Blood where apparently he will be safe there and at

this point Percy is starting to realize that things aren't all normal in his life and there may be some secrets about his upbringing or about his birth that his mother has not told him however before they are able to arrive at this Camp the Minotaur Takes her and she vanishes in a Flash of light Percy basically thinks his mother has been killed at this stage Percy somehow manages to kill the monster and he passes out right afterwards is the last few paragraphs that conclude this scene the last thing I remember is collapsing

on a wooden porch looking up at a ceiling fan circling above me moths flying around a yellow light and the stern faces of a familiar looking bearded man and a pretty girl her blonde hair curled like a princess's they both looked down at me and the girl said he's the one he must be and you can see here this comes on page 59 of my addition about 16% of the way through the story this then leads into the entering of the new realm this is where your protagonist is taken from their Ordinary World and

thrust into the extraordinary world of your story now Ordinary World extraordinary world you can just take those terms as metaphorical in some stories there will be a very literal very clear transition between the Ordinary World and the extraordinary world something like Harry Potter is a good example Harry goes from the Muggle world into the Wizarding World but in other stories like maybe a detective story where there is a crime that comes along that is sort of more brutal or more violent or more devious than

anything the detective has dealt with before that can also signal a transformation from The Ordinary World where the main character kind of understands the rules into the extraordinary world where the character is off balance they're out of their comfort zone and there're so much more danger and threat as a result of that so in the case of Percy Jackson this transition occurs when Percy wakes up in Camp Half Blood and he discovers that he is a demigod he is the son of a human mother and one of the Greek gods is his

father father or mother he doesn't quite know at this stage who his Godly parent actually is but he basically learns that all the Greek myths are real and the Greek gods are alive in modern day America he's told that the big three Gods so Zeus Poseidon and Hades they are not allowed to have kids because there's this dangerous prophecy that if one of their kids gets to the age of 16 they will destroy Olympus and he is introduced to the other demigods in the camp including Annabeth who is a girl

who sort of helps retrieve him after his initial confrontation with the minor she is a child of Athena and initially she's a little bit kind of edgy towards him another key figure he meets is Luke who is a child of Hermes and Luke is a bit of a older Mentor figure who takes Percy under his wing and helps to sort of introduce him into Camp life under Luke's guidance Percy is tested to try and find out which God he belongs to but unfortunately he sucks at almost everything here so he still continues to

feel like a huge Misfit next we move on to the fourth story structure point which is the antagonist threatening your main character so this is where pressure is applied to your main character typically through either the sort of introduction or just some kind of key action from your antagonist so you might have actually introduced your antagonist earlier on maybe you even introduced it in the hook of your story right at the start but this is your opportunity to tighten the screws on your main character and to elevate the level of

By ripping off J.R.R Tolkien of course! Now some of you may think that the genre of fantasy is an excuse to free one's imagination to create truly alien and bizarre races.

Halflings are boring and they will have no place in our fantasy plot since our conflict with the dark lord will be resolved in a one on one duel with a teenager who is secretly the heir to the human kingdom. We can't have meek, ordinary folk actually rise to the occasion and selflessly risk their

happy lives to save the world. After all, average people can't accomplish anything and the fantasy genre certainly wouldn't waste time pandering to those people, now would it? Why would they need an escapist fantasy? Now we have all the fantasy races we need to populate our very original and creative fantasy world. Some might worry that we stray into unfortunate implications by creating 'races' who have specific 'abilities'. Especially when we say that some races, like say blond hair blue eyed elves, are better

than others. But don't worry. No one calls anyone else a racist on the internet.

Hey Subfuries. Fantasy stories are known for a lot of things: vague, often contrived prophecies; gallant, amazingly gifted chosen one heroes with no parents, because they're inconvenient for the plot; and lots and lots of mythical races. But arguably, the thing that really sets fantasy apart from other genres is magic: its role in the world you create, how characters can use it to solve problems, and the problems it can create. Oftentimes, a really unique magic system is what sets one fantasy story apart from another.

In writing your fantasy novels, something to think about is how Hard or Soft you want your magic system to be. Now we have to thank our Lord and Savior of Hard magic systems, Brandon Sanderson, for popularizing the terms Hard and Soft, but what do they mean? This video will be delving deep into Hard magic systems so I'll only be lightly touching on what a Soft magic system is, but broadly speaking: Soft magic systems often have a vague, undefined, or mysterious set of rules and limitations to being used.

If you like fantasy, then you've definitely seen this in Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings: everyone knows Gandalf can do wizardy things with his pointy hat and his staff, but when it comes down to the specific limitations of what he can and can't do, Gandalf tends to skimp on the details. [Gandalf Europop Nod meme music] A Hard magic system, on the other hand, has clearly defined rules, consequences, and limitations that govern what one can or cannot do with magic; that your hero can use telekinesis,

but they can only use it on things they could realistically lift themselves, and the things have to be within 10 metres of them. A great example of a Hard magic system is Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood, which if you haven't seen, has amazing characters, world-building and story structure. If you enjoyed Avatar The Last Airbender, there's a good chance you might enjoy that. In Fullmetal, they call magic "alchemy", and it's governed strictly by: which trust me, you'll get to know very well as you watch the series

because they repeat it at the start of Every. Single. Episode. For example, Alphonse transforms all of the pieces of a broken radio into a working radio; all of the pieces are there, they just have to be put in the right place and order in order to work again. Alchemy never ever breaks that first rule, the viewer knows pretty well what the characters can or can't do in any given circumstance. Now, your story can have a magic system that is anywhere on the spectrum from Soft to Hard and both styles have their merits and  limitations for different kinds of stories,

but let's talk about Hard magic today. Sanderson wrote essays on what he calls his Three Rules of Magic, but the most important one for Hard magic systems is the first: Writing is all about how you set up problems and conflicts, and how they're resolved in a way that that makes for a good story. If we have no idea what Gandalf can do and he just solved every problem the Fellowship has with random unseen-before magical spells and moments of tension, then it wouldn't be a satisfying resolution,

and feels like the author is just writing -- -- and expecting you to be happy with a clear deus ex machina. [Meme returns] Sticking to Sanderson's first rule in Hard magic systems means the reader understands what characters can or can't do, their capabilities; and are always thinking about how magic can be used to solve problems, within those strict rules that you laid out Magic becomes a defined tool that doesn't feel cheap to use because it's not screaming -- -- at the reader.

[You know what's up] Readers can feel cheated by Soft magic because it's much harder to predict where it can be used, or what it can do, but Hard magic allows the reader to feel much more a part of the story; aligning themselves with the characters as they earnestly predict how magic could be used in any given circumstance. In Avatar The Last Airbender -- and forgive me for using it as the benchmark for all things good and holy in writing -- -- the bending magic system is relatively Hard;

it's not all that mysterious, with the exception of an occasional new alternate bending style thrown in and the rules are relatively clear. It's established numerous times throughout the series that water can be bent from a variety of sources, it doesn't just have to be water flowing in a river, say, but you can bend it from trees, vines, and even human blood So it's a logical and satisfying conclusion to have Katara escape prison by water bending her body sweat the viewer could have figured it out just as Katara

did, after all, the human body is full of water. But how do you actually design a Hard magic system? Firstly, you have to keep in mind its Predictability. Typically, the harder your magic system, the more specific you have to be about its rules and consequences. Soft magic can be mysterious and unpredictable, but: That if our gallant hero with his suave look and 11 inch wand does magical action [x], he can expect magical consequence [y]. Now this doesn't mean that your Hard magic can't have the possibility of disastrous or unpredicted

consequences, should the magic go horribly wrong, but it does mean that those unpredictable effects will often come from the character's lack of knowledge, mistake, or misuse of the intended magic, not because the magic is inherently unpredictable. Once again, my baby Fullmetal Alchemist demonstrates this perfectly, when an attempt to bring someone back from the dead creates a ghoulish monster and destroys Alphonse's entire physical body, not because the magic itself was unpredictable, but because they didn't understand The Law of

Equivalent Exchange, the rule that governs all alchemy. While Sanderson didn't say this explicitly, I do feel that the guidelines for designing Hard magic systems are best encompassed fundamentally in his essay, "The Second Law of Magic". If you want to read it in more detail, there's a link down in the description below to it. Seems pretty simple, right? That Harry Potter's magic is limited because he can only cast spells when he has a wand -- though, later on we do learn that

wand-less magic is a thing for, like, level 99 wizards with really cool hats. [The return] Hard magic systems often boil down to three things: These essentially create the rules your magical characters have to obey. What limits are there on their powers? Can your suave hero mind-control people, but only as long as they can see them and they're naked? The most common form of limitation is a vaguely defined limit of strength, or training, or mental acumen of the practitioner. Avatar the Last Airbender is kind of like this.

There's no explicit limit to how much fire a person can conjure, or how strong a wind they can muster, but we know it's kind of limited by their training, willpower, strength, and talent. Think of it as the rule of: If you're really trying to differentiate your Hard magic system from this common trope, then think about not relying on this particular limitation, but maybe something else. Perhaps certain powers can be negated or are affected by certain things in the environment around them, like the Moon, certain plants, or minerals.

That way, your magician has to be aware of their surroundings at all times, or it can be used against them by their enemies. Secondly: Weaknesses in magic systems can create interesting dynamics in a story where magic would usually make a character a lot more powerful than those around them. Maybe they can transform into a werewolf at will, but that makes them vulnerable to silver bullets though, once again, making these limitations to your magic too simple can be ... uninteresting. Don't just give your super suave hero with fantastic hair

and gorgeous eyes a Kryptonite factor that completely incapacitates them. If you have multiple different powers in your story, it could be interesting to have the use of one power making them more vulnerable to another, so your character has to be cautious about using their powers around someone who could take advantage of that. At its heart, I personally feel that: Finally and thirdly, perhaps the most common way that people create rules for their magic system is through magic costing something. Fullmetal Alchemist requires

the exact materials to turn [x] into [y]. In a lot of series, the magician requires certain materials for their spell or enchantment. "Bone ... of the father ... " " ... unwillingly ... given." "Flesh ... of the servant ... " " ... willingly ... sacrificed." "Blood ... of the enemy ... " " ... forcibly ... " [Harry screams] " ... taken." In Harry Potter, this ritual had costs in terms of ingredients as well as the way the ingredients had to be acquired.

But perhaps the most common magical cost is that of bodily energy. In The Wheel of Time and The Inheritance Cycle, doing something with magic exhausts you, which is fine until you try and be TOO magically heroic, and you overdose on magical heroin and DIE. Magic causing fatigue is so common because it's an easy way to separate the strong from the weak. A powerful magician doesn't flinch as she vanquishes an army, while a weak one collapses from trying to zap a fly. It'll ask for a lot of wiggle room

for the author, because you can make it so that your hero has just enough energy to do impressive magical thing [x] without much more justification than a short training montage beforehand. but you've got to be careful about how you use this cost: We've already talked about how Hard magic systems require a level of predictability and consistency and the exhaustion cost can challenge their predictability and suspension of belief if not used wisely. One of my favorite examples of a magical cost is

actually from one of the softest fantasy magic systems, in A Song of Ice and Fire. In that, Beric Dondarrion is brought back to life dozens of times using magic and it changes him. George RR Martin described it as such: Coming back from the dead costs Beric Dondarrion something of himself -- what, precisely, we're never told, but it's visible in the character in his books. "Pieces of you get chipped away." Look for unique ways to make your magic cost, if you want to distinguish your magic system from others.

Maybe manipulating the element of Earth causes plants to die around you. The ramifications of these effects could be widespread and fascinating to explore: if this kind of magic was common, would it be outlawed to protect the crops and forests? Interestingly, both Avatar and Harry Potter have very little cost in terms of their magic. The exhaustion that the Avatar characters experience seems to be primarily from the physical exercise they get doing what essentially amounts to martial arts, and while we do see that it requires effort at certain

points, exhaustion never plays the large cost-like role that we see in The Wheel of Time or The Belgariad, where overusing magic can kill you. Likewise, casting spells in Harry Potter very rarely seems to draw on the strength of the caster. There are vague lines in the books that refer to powerful spells requiring powerful magic, but it rarely acts as a true cost to the witch or the wizard. The reason for this in both series, I think, is that their magic systems are restricted heavily by limitations rather than cost.

Bending is limited pretty strictly by ability and practice, while magical ability is limited by knowledge and skill. It really just depends on which kind of rules you want your Hard magic system to rely on. Finally: You need to pick a style for your Hard magic system, and this can be a lot of fun. Typically speaking, Hard magic systems need to be more specific about this than Soft magic. Maybe you want a theurgical magic system, where your characters channel the power of Gods, angels, and demons --

[Once more, with heart] -- or maybe they need special magical devices, like various items of glamorous jewelry; or it requires blood and sacrifice; or maybe they're tapping into the ubiquitous Force that permeates everything and everyone conveniently. I often find that writers focus on designing the style of their magic system more than the other parts we talked about before, and while it's a lot of fun to design the aesthetics of it, it's the -- -- that will play into the conflicts, problems, and

character interactions of the story the most. But of course, as I always say, there's no right way to write, and it's all up to how you feel that you work best. These guidelines will work for some people, and they won't work for others. This is going to be a three-part writing series on magic systems, and next time, I want to talk to you about Soft magic systems: how to design them, and their place in your fictional, fantastical world. I hope this helped, and if it did, please give it a like

and leave me a comment down below. My question of the day is: What is your magic system like? How would you design one? If you like what I make, please consider supporting me on Patreon for as little as $1.00. You can get early videos, as well as plenty of other perks. In the meantime, come follow me on Twitter, Wattpad, Facebook, email me stuff you've made at the address, or links in the description below. That is all from me today. Stay nerdy, subfuries. I will see you in the future.

I asked 400 readers what is the best way to start a fantasy novel I'm about to share with you the 10 most common responses along with drawing from my own experience as a fantasy author to show you how you can use this data to write better openings in your own fantasy novel we had over 28,000 words worth of responses for this survey and as we go through them you'll learn which of these 10 starts is my personal favorite along with some advice for implementing these openings effectively in your own writing

you will also notice that pretty much none of these responses mention a common piece of opening writing advice which is often thrown around online which made me feel very validated because it's something that I have always pushed back against but we'll get to that later let's start with number 10 Begin by introducing the magic system so one respondent said give me a magic system with flaws limitations costs and some insane functionality I want to see an assassin who can change the direction

gravity affects him like in The Stormlight Archive A Healer who can mind control anyone she sees like in six of crows or a man who commits suicide by creating a mountain around himself like in The Wheel of Time all very good examples another respondent said I think the most important thing is you have to show something Fantastical this is fantasy show off something unique that will keep me hooked this could be a part of the magic system an amazing setting detail strange creatures anything that shows promise now in terms of my

thoughts on this not every fantasy novel actually needs a magic system there are plenty of great fantasy novels with zero magic in them whatsoever it's typically called the low fantasy genre I think that's a slightly derogatory term personally but if you do have a really cool and really unique Magic system in your story then it is a fantastic idea to show a slice of that to readers early on notice that I say a slice you don't want to just overwhelm readers with you know 20 pages of explanation around how

all the magic Works rather you are much better off just giving readers a tantalizing glimmer or glimpse of what the magic is capable of and then leave a lot of mystery around what uses the magic could be put to or what other abilities might be contained in that magic later on in your story now if you are going to show your magic system early in your fantasy novel there is one big tip I have for you and this is going to help you a lot with your writing in your opening try to suggest or hint at the tough choices your magic system

might Force characters to make later on in your story a fantastic example of this is let's imagine you have a magic where you can enchant magical robes for your characters to use okay that's all right that could be interesting but what if the only way to enchant those magical robes was you had to sacrifice The Souls of dozens or even hundreds of humans to some demonic entity that is basically the setup of one of the many Magic systems in Blackstone Heart by Michael R Fletcher and as soon as that idea is

introduced you as a reader just have a tremendous amount of intrigue and curiosity around how that is going to play out because you can see the difficult choices and the tough dilemas that that magic system could force the character to enter into later in the story so if you can establish early on that your magic is going to create hard choices for your character later it will create tremendous suspense and tension for your reader the next best way to start your fantasy novel according to this survey is with the antagonist this

response actually surprised me a little I was pleasantly intrigued to see this here because while I wasn't immediately thinking of it myself as you'll see from the some of these answers here is actually a very compelling opening for a couple of different reasons so we had one respondent saying oh I think it's fun to first introduce the bad guy doing something evil or their backstory before they become the villain then introduce the hero afterwards another respondent said I love it when we open with the

introduction of the villain or antagonist rather than the protagonist in my opinion this works really well because you can build tension and Stakes right from the start I have a lot of thoughts on that we'll get to in a moment another respondent said I love the villain doing an evil thing to set the stakes and to give me the promise of the villain's defeat then you can introduce the hero later and there was one particularly great example which a respondent sent in which I want to share in full with you here for example the

first chapter of Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire one of my favorite opening chapters of all time it sets a darker tone for the book with the death of the caretaker if you don't know the context of this the opening from Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire which is the fourth book in the series begins with uh a caretaker basically hearing a conversation between Voldemort and and his servant Peter pedigree and it's only at the very end of this chapter that you see that Voldemort is this kind of

horribly shrunken and um disfigured little baby but he has somehow managed to come back into a Corporal form after sort of being a spirit for most of the first half of the Harry Potter series so it sets a darker tone for the book with the death of that very caretaker Frank rest in peace Frank um sets up it vm's plan for his return by showing him getting more powerful and having allies and then this is probably the most important part it hints at this deeper connection between Harry and Voldemort

by Harry being able to witness the event in his dreams so what's really crazy here is I had not had the Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire opening on my mind at all in terms of a great example of how to start your fantasy novel as soon as I read this response in the survey I remembered how damn good that opening is and it is my favorite opening out of all seven of the Harry Potter novels interestingly it's pretty much one of the only ones that starts from the antagonist perspective you also have

in uh Harry Potter and the Half Blood Prince that sort of starts with Snape making this unbreakable oath with some other um dark wizards but I really love the Goblet of Fire opening for all of the reasons that this respondent has shared here the really nice thing about starting with the antagonist is you create a information gap between what you know as the reader or what you're telling to the reader and what your protagonist actually knows so if you're starting from for example with the

antagonist uh creating a plan to go off and assassinate the main character and then you cut to the main character and they are living their life completely oblivious of the fact that an assassin is heading for them there is tremendous suspense there because there is a huge information gap between what you know as the reader and what the character actually knows we're going to have a huge amount of worry when is the Assassin going to arrive how is the Assassin going to attack them will the protagonist be able to survive and so

when you start with the antagonist in your story you can maybe then go 100 Pages 200 Pages maybe even more without your antagonist showing up but all throughout those first 100 Pages first 200 Pages whatever it is there will be a tremendous amount of suspense you can almost think about starting with the antagonist as a way to pull back on a lucky band and then keep that tension there as the reader gets into the protagonist and they're wondering this whole time when is this lucky band going to release and go flying forward by

comparison if you just write a story where you maybe don't introduce the antagonist until page 200 then you don't really have suspense in those first 200 Pages you just probably have shock when the antagonist finally arrives and so that's why this kind of opening can be quite powerful if you are writing a story where maybe there's a lot of focus on the protagonist life but the main antagonist does not enter the picture until later on and of course you can fall into the Trap of drawing out the

suspense too long in my very first novel that I wrote the Aon Academy which I started writing when I was 14 I didn't even introduce my antagonist until the fifth last chapter of the book and it wasn't because I was doing anything clever where I set up all the suspense from them earlier I just genuinely like did not realize that I needed to introduce my antagonist earlier in the story so you can definitely take this tip um to the negative extreme now if you are going to start with the antagonist in your fantasy novel there

is a very critical mistake to avoid and this is something that I've seen with a lot of the writers I've worked with at this point I've worked with over 80 writers for some of those I edited their entire novels for writers I worked with them in my fantasy outlining boot camp and in still others I ran them through a live first chapter critique workshop and one of the common mistakes that I've actually seen quite a few fantasy writers make is they have some kind of conflict or fight between the antagonist

and the protagonist early on I'm talking maybe even chapter one and the antagonist is defeated by the main character the problem with that kind of opening is that if you are then butting the main character up against that same antagonist later in the story and the antagonist has not increased in their power or threat levels and the main character hasn't really changed either there won't be any real tension or uncertainty for the reader because we've already seen how this equation resolves

before so you do have to be careful about these openings where you have both your antagonist and your protagonist right away unless it's something where your protagonist manages to just Escape but it's very clear to us that the antagonist threat and power is far superior this is why in many cases great ant antagonist openings will just have the antagonist doing something badass by themselves perhaps to some disposable Side characters so that you immediately establish their threat without worrying

dialogue has such a powerful sense of immediacy and there's actually a very particular scientific reason for this broadly speaking in your story you have two types of Pros the first type is concrete pros this is when you're describing something that actually is for example action beats setting descriptions sentence like the dog smelled of mud and wet fur is a concrete description it's describing something that is actually there the second type of Pros is abstract pros this is when you're describing something that is not

literally there in front of the character's eyes so these tend to be things like character thoughts or emotions or interpretations or characters remembering some past event for example the sentence the muddy dog reminded John of the puppy his parents had once adopted that is an abstract sentence because it is a character interpreting what's in front of him and remembering a scene or a moment from the past so as a rule of thumb concrete Pros takes place in the present and it pushes the story forward abstract Pros often

times takes place in the past or it's about a character backfilling or backtracking to explain something that happened before and usually it doesn't always move the story forward there are some exceptions emotions can be something that is abstract but might actually progress where the story is going the reason I bring that up is because you generally want to good balance of concrete and Abstract Pros in your novel but what's fantastic about dialogue is that it is always so concrete because it is something that is

actually happening in the events of your story and therefore there is a sense of immediacy and momentum and progression whenever dialogue is unfolding on a page dialogue is something that is happening right now and it pushes us chronologically forward through the narrative it's also such a powerful tool to establish characters goals personality quirks and other key traits now having said that there is a common dialogue mistake that new fantasy writers often make in the start of their story and it is to use as you know

dialogue so this is where one character says to the other well as you know Bob the mountain over our town has not exploded for thousands of years so we should be safe as we go out here to plow these farmlands so as you know dialogue is when characters explain things that they already know to each other and it's done purely for the benefit of readers the problem with as you know dialogue is that it feels fake it feels artificial and the reader will feel like you are talking down to them and it just makes

your story feel dumbed down and stupid and of course there's a lot of other dialogue mistakes to avoid uh throughout your entire fantasy novel but that is probably the biggest one I see in the opening of most stories now I'm actually thinking about running a live fantasy dialogue workshop at some point in the near future so if that sounds like it would be interesting for you to get my personal feedback on your dialogues on a dialogue scene from your story then make sure you comment down down below and

Applying the Video Advice to Your Story
You’ve built a massive, intricate world. The transcripts you’ve shared are packed with craft advice that can help you turn that world into a compelling narrative. I’ve extracted the most relevant lessons and applied them directly to your project—pointing out where your current plans align, where you might be walking into common traps, and how to adjust.

I. The Nine Common Plot Mistakes – How They Apply to You
1. Beating the Antagonist Too Early
Video says: If your protagonist defeats the main antagonist in the first few chapters, there’s no suspense when they fight again later.

Your situation: Your protagonist’s main antagonist is Lucius Varro (the regressor). In your outline, the Frostfang Incident happens in Year 2. The protagonist survives but does not defeat Varro—he merely escapes and is nearly expelled. Varro remains powerful, with political backing and his regressor knowledge. Later, in the Champion’s Gauntlet semifinal, the protagonist does defeat Varro in a duel. That’s near the end of the Academy arc, not the beginning.

Verdict: You’re safe. Varro’s early appearance does not end in his defeat; he remains a threat. The duel defeat is a climax, which is appropriate. However, note: Varro’s regressor knowledge means he might have other ways to retaliate. Keep him dangerous even after losing a public match—perhaps he uses political maneuvering, or his knowledge of future events, to stay a threat.

2. Repetitive Scene Formats
Video says: New writers often use the same type of scene over and over (e.g., characters talking in a house). Vary scene formats to keep readers engaged.

Your situation: Your outline has a good variety: tavern scenes, hunting scenes, guard training, magical beast attack, academy classes, expeditions (Frostfang), competitions (Maze Hunt, Champion’s Gauntlet), sabotage and political intrigue, border war skirmishes, final defense. That’s a healthy mix. However, be careful not to overuse “conversation in a room” scenes in the early chapters. Use your early scenes to show action and conflict, not just exposition.

Action item: When you write the childhood scenes, ensure each has a distinct format: the first tavern scene (character moment), the first hunt (action/failure), the guard training (mentorship), the magical beast attack (high stakes survival). That’s four different scene types already.

3. Passive Protagonist
Video says: A passive protagonist is one the story happens to, rather than one who makes active choices. Readers should feel the story begins when the protagonist makes their first truly active choice.

Your situation: Your protagonist starts as a curious boy who chooses to learn the spear (sneaking to guard drills, accepting Harald’s training). He chooses to hunt, chooses to throw the rope to the adventurers, chooses to beg the cleric for magic lessons. At the academy, he chooses to befriend outsiders, chooses to compete, chooses to defy Varro. His death is a choice to stay and defend the village.

Verdict: He is active throughout. The only potential passive stretch might be the very early childhood (ages 5–8) where he’s just observing. But that’s setup, and it’s brief. Ensure that by the time he meets Harald, he’s already making choices.

Action item: In the early childhood scenes, give him small active choices—e.g., he chooses to give stew to a tired traveler without being asked, showing agency even as a child.

4. No Consistent Through‑Line
Video says: A story needs a core conflict summarized in one sentence. Without it, the plot meanders.

Your situation: Your story has a through‑line: a commoner with no special advantages builds himself into a versatile fighter through grit and ingenuity, and in the process challenges a world built on privilege, ultimately choosing to die for something he believes in. That’s strong. But within the plot, the conflict shifts: early life is about survival and learning; academy years are about proving himself against nobles; adventuring years are about navigating war and moral choices; his death is about protecting the innocent. Each phase has a distinct goal, but they all connect to the theme of an unspecial person mattering.

Potential risk: The academy years could feel disconnected from the later war if the through‑line isn’t reinforced. Make sure Varro’s rivalry ties into the larger political conflict (his father is a general; his regressor knowledge relates to the war). Also, the Frostfang Incident should have consequences that echo into the war (e.g., General Varro’s grudge, or the wyrm’s heart crystal being used in the war effort).

5. Soggy Middle
Video says: The middle (Act 2) often lacks progression. Using a seven‑point plot structure (hook, plot turn 1, pinch point 1, midpoint, pinch point 2, plot turn 2, resolution) helps.

Your situation: Your academy years (Years 2–4) are your “middle.” You have clear pinch points: Frostfang Incident (pinch 1), the sabotage campaign (rising action), the Champion’s Gauntlet (midpoint/climax of that arc). That’s good structure. The adventuring years (between academy and final stand) could become soggy if you don’t have clear events. You have a few outlined: first freelance contract, meeting Renard, border war escalation. But you might need more.

Action item: For the adventuring years, map out a few key missions that each force him to grow and connect to the larger conflict. Use the seven‑point structure for that section as well: hook (his first contract), plot turn 1 (he chooses to work as neutral scout), pinch 1 (a war crime he witnesses), midpoint (reunion with friends, realization he can’t stay neutral), pinch 2 (he learns of Thornwood Hollow’s danger), plot turn 2 (he decides to defend it), resolution (his death).

6. Weak Consequences
Video says: Writers often avoid punishing characters. Adversity reveals depth. Ask “what is the worst possible thing that could happen?”

Your situation: You’ve built consequences: he nearly dies in the hunting incident, the Frostfang Incident kills people and traumatizes him, his gear is sabotaged, his father dies while he’s away, and ultimately he dies. That’s good. However, consider emotional consequences: does he carry guilt from Frostfang? Does his father’s death affect his later choices? Does his unrequited attraction to Lena leave any mark?

Action item: Add a scene where he wrestles with guilt after Frostfang—perhaps he has nightmares, or he avoids the alchemist who was injured. Show him carrying his father’s knife and thinking about him during the final stand. These small emotional beats will make the consequences feel real.

7. Misaligning Promise, Progress, Payoff (The 3 P’s)
Video says: The opening promises a certain kind of story; the middle must progress toward that; the payoff must satisfy the promise.

Your situation: Your promise is “a commoner rises through skill and integrity in a world of privilege, and his choices matter.” The progress is his training, competitions, and moral decisions. The payoff is his death and legacy. That’s aligned. But ensure the early chapters don’t promise something you later abandon—for example, if you open with a gritty survival scene, don’t shift to a lighthearted academy comedy.

8. Puttering Endings
Video says: Resolving plot threads one by one over several chapters can make the ending feel slow. Better to knot them together into one climactic moment.

Your situation: His death is one moment, but there are threads that resolve after his death: the village’s escape, Renard’s grief, his friends’ reactions, the academy reforms, Mira’s plaque. These are epilogue material, which is fine. The key is to make his death itself the knot where many threads converge: his rivalry with Varro (Varro’s forces are part of the attacking army?), his relationship with Renard (they fight together), his skills (he uses everything he learned), his moral choice (he stays). That’s a strong knot.

Action item: Consider having Varro’s unit be the one attacking the village. That way the personal rivalry ends at the same moment as his death. It also gives Varro a chance for reflection later.

9. Luck That Helps the Protagonist
Video says: Coincidences that help the protagonist feel cheap. Luck should help the antagonist, or the protagonist should earn their wins through skill.

Your situation: Your protagonist’s successes come from training, preparation, and clever tactics—not luck. The one exception might be his survival of the magical beast attack (the adventurers arriving). But that’s early and establishes that he’s not invincible. Later, his victories are earned. Good.

II. Structuring Your Novel (The Nine‑Point Plot)
The video outlines a nine‑point structure (Hook, Inciting Incident, Entering New Realm, Antagonist Threatens, Midpoint Revelation, Amplified Pressure, Darkest Low, Climax, Closing Image). Let’s map your story onto it:

Point	Your Story
Hook	Childhood tavern scene; he’s observant, works hard, wants more than the tavern.
Inciting Incident	The magical beast attack; he nearly dies and sees magic for the first time. He decides to learn magic.
Entering New Realm	He goes to the academy—new world of nobles, halls, magic. He’s an outsider.
Antagonist Threatens	Lucius Varro emerges as a rival. The Frostfang Incident escalates the threat.
Midpoint Revelation	The Champion’s Gauntlet semifinal? Or maybe the moment he realizes Varro is a regressor and that he can’t just out‑fight him—he must out‑think him. Alternatively, the midpoint could be his decision to work as a neutral scout after graduation, shifting from personal ambition to a larger purpose.
Amplified Pressure	The Border War intensifies; he witnesses atrocities; his neutrality is tested.
Darkest Low	He learns the village is in danger; he’s wounded; the choice to stay may be the low point (he knows he’ll likely die).
Climax	His final stand; he holds off the soldiers long enough for the villagers to escape; he dies.
Closing Image	Mira’s plaque; the village remembers; the fox‑kin ceremony; his legacy lives on.
Note: Your midpoint needs to be a clear, reflective moment where the protagonist understands something about himself. Perhaps it’s after the Champion’s Gauntlet, when he realizes he’s not fighting for fame but for something larger. Or it could be the moment he decides to work as a neutral scout, rejecting national allegiances. Choose one and make it a quiet, contemplative scene.

III. Character Arc (Ghost, Lie, Want, Need, Truth)
The video describes a positive character arc: Ghost → Lie → Want → Need → Truth.

Your protagonist’s arc:

Ghost: As a child, he’s invisible—a tavern‑keeper’s son, no one expects anything of him. He sees nobles and adventurers treated better. He learns that the world rewards birth, not effort.

Lie: “I have to become someone important to matter. I need power and recognition to be worth something.”

Want: To prove himself—to become a great fighter, to be respected, to earn enough to help his family.

Need: To realize that his worth is not in titles or fame, but in the choices he makes and the people he protects. He matters because he chooses to matter.

Truth: “A commoner can matter by standing up for what’s right, even if no one sings songs about it.”

His death is the ultimate expression of this truth: he dies for a village no one important cares about, and that act matters more than any tournament victory.

Action item: Make sure his lie is articulated in the early chapters. Perhaps he overhears a noble say “commoners are only useful as fodder,” and that plants the seed.

IV. Writing Habits and Editing
The video emphasizes that writing a first draft is about “shoveling sand into the sandbox.” You already have an incredibly detailed outline (sandbox). Now you need to start shoveling.

Practical next steps based on video advice:

Pick your point of view. The video suggests a single POV for a first novel. Your story could be told entirely from the protagonist’s perspective (close third person). That would keep it focused and manageable.

Use the 5‑minute rule. Commit to writing for five minutes each day. Often you’ll keep going.

Track your word count. Gamify the process.

End each session before you exhaust ideas. Leave a sentence unfinished so you know where to start next.

Don’t edit as you go. Get the sand in first. You have an outline; trust it.

V. The Magic System: Hard vs. Soft
The video discusses hard vs. soft magic systems. Your system is hard—physics‑based, with clear limits (telekinesis range, mana pool, chain state mechanics). That’s good for a protagonist who solves problems through clever application of rules.

One caution: The video warns that hard magic can become predictable. Your protagonist’s creativity (using physics principles) keeps it fresh. Ensure you introduce new applications of the chain and telekinesis throughout the story, not all at once. Show him discovering a new technique in each major conflict.

VI. The Cultural and Worldbuilding Advice
The video’s sarcastic section about ripping off Tolkien is a warning against lazy worldbuilding. You’ve done the opposite: you’ve built distinct cultures, each with their own magic and politics, and you’ve tied them to real‑world history without being derivative. That’s excellent.

One note: The video warns against making races “fundamentally evil.” Your “fourth party” (beast‑kin, elementals, etc.) are explicitly not evil—they are victims. That’s a good subversion.

VII. Final Synthesis: What to Focus on Now
Based on all the video advice and your worldbuilding, here’s a refined priority list:

Write the four childhood scenes (tavern, first hunt, Harald’s gift, magical beast attack). Make sure they establish his active nature and the lie he believes.

Write the Frostfang Incident as a full chapter. Use it as your first major pinch point. Show Varro’s threat and the protagonist’s resilience.

Write the Champion’s Gauntlet semifinal as the midpoint of the academy arc. Use it to show his truth beginning to emerge (he fights for honor, not just victory).

Write the final stand as the climax. Ensure it knots together multiple threads.

Write the epilogue to show legacy.

Along the way, use the seven‑point plot structure for each arc. Keep the protagonist active. Ensure consequences (emotional and physical) are felt. And remember the video’s core message: your first draft just needs to exist. You can polish later.

The Complete Guide to Writing a Fantasy Story: From Idea to Finished Novel
This guide synthesizes everything from the writing advice videos you shared, applied directly to the world and story you’ve built. Whether you’re starting from scratch or refining a first draft, these steps will help you structure your work, avoid common pitfalls, and turn your rich world into a compelling narrative.

I. Phase One: Finding Your Story
1. Choose the Right Idea
What you’ve done: You already have a clear, passionate idea—a commoner with no special advantages who builds himself through skill and dies meaningfully. You’ve also identified the tropes you love (school story, underdog, found family, tactical combat) and merged them.

The key: The best story is the one you’re obsessed with. You’ve already passed the “shower test”—you keep thinking about it.

Action: Commit to this idea. Don’t worry about marketability; write for yourself first.

2. Define Your Scope
Advice from videos: For a first novel, keep it manageable—one point‑of‑view, a standalone story (or a self‑contained first book).

Your story: You have a single protagonist with a complete arc from childhood to death. That’s ideal. Avoid adding multiple POVs in the first draft unless necessary. If you later want to show other perspectives, you can add them in revision.

II. Phase Two: Building the Core (The Hourglass Method)
Step 1: Explore the “Suburb” – Brain Dump Everything
What to do: Write down all your ideas: characters, scenes, magic, world details, themes, emotions. Use a notebook or digital doc.

You already did this: Your conversation history is your brain dump—thousands of words of ideas.

Step 2: Find Your Story’s Core – Premise and Theme
A. Craft a One‑Sentence Premise
Purpose: Clarifies the external conflict and hooks readers.

Example from your story: A tavern‑keeper’s son with no magical talent builds himself into a master of a shape‑shifting chain weapon, only to discover that in a world of nobles, prodigies, and regressors, being unspecial is its own kind of strength—and his final choice to protect the forgotten will cost him everything.

Action: Refine this into a sharp, compelling sentence. It can evolve as you write.

B. Develop Your Theme
Definition: A moral argument about how to live, explored through the story.

Your theme: A person’s worth is not in titles or fame, but in the choices they make and the people they protect.

Category: This fits “I can see all sides”—it’s a truth that can be argued from different perspectives (e.g., some characters believe power is what matters; the protagonist shows otherwise).

Action: Write your theme on a sticky note and keep it visible as you outline and write.

Step 3: Create a One‑Page Guiding Principles Document
Include: Premise, theme, protagonist’s ghost/lie/want/need/truth, a high‑level synopsis, and any key worldbuilding notes.

Your version: You already have this in summary form. Condense it to one page for quick reference.

III. Phase Three: Outline – The Hourglass Expands
1. Structure Your Character Arc (Positive Arc)
Ghost: Childhood invisibility; sees the world rewards birth over effort.

Lie: “I have to become someone important to matter.”

Want: To prove himself, earn respect, help his family.

Need: To realize his worth is in his choices, not recognition.

Truth: “A commoner can matter by standing up for what’s right, even if no one sings songs about it.”

2. Map the Plot Using the Nine‑Point Structure
Adapt the structure to your story’s phases:

Point	Your Story Application
Hook	Childhood tavern scenes; protagonist’s curiosity and work ethic.
Inciting Incident	Magical beast attack; he nearly dies and sees magic; decides to learn.
Entering the New Realm	Academy life; introduced to halls, nobles, and his friends.
Antagonist Threatens	Lucius Varro emerges as rival; Frostfang Incident nearly kills him.
Midpoint Revelation	Champion’s Gauntlet semifinal; he realizes he fights for more than himself.
Amplified Pressure	Border War; he witnesses atrocities; his neutrality is tested.
Darkest Low	Thornwood Hollow is threatened; he’s wounded; he knows he may die.
Climax	His final stand; he holds the pass, dies, but villagers escape.
Closing Image	Mira’s plaque; fox‑kin ceremony; legacy lives on.
Note: The midpoint is crucial—it’s where the protagonist stops reacting and starts acting with deeper understanding. For you, it could be the moment after the Champion’s Gauntlet when he realizes he doesn’t want to serve any nation, or when he first encounters the fox‑kin and sees humanity in them.

3. Fill in the Scenes with Variety
Avoid repetitive scene formats. Ensure a mix: action, dialogue, introspection, travel, competition, stealth, etc.

Your variety is good. Just double‑check that early chapters aren’t all “conversations in a room.”

4. Apply the Seven‑Point Plot Structure to Each Arc
The video’s seven‑point structure can be used for each major section (Academy years, Adventuring years). For example, the Academy arc:

Opening: He arrives, meets friends, struggles.

Plot Turn 1: He discovers the chain and starts building his style.

Pinch Point 1: Frostfang Incident.

Midpoint: He realizes Varro is a regressor and that skill alone won’t win.

Pinch Point 2: Sabotage campaign; his gear is tampered with.

Plot Turn 2: He decides to face Varro in the Champion’s Gauntlet, using his own methods.

Resolution: He wins, but refuses to join any faction; graduates.

IV. Phase Four: Writing the First Draft
1. Mindset
“Shovel sand into the sandbox.” Don’t edit as you go. Just get the words down.

Focus on today’s step. Don’t worry about publication or book four.

Enjoy the process. You’re passionate about this story—let that carry you.

2. Build a Daily Writing Habit
Find your energy apex. Experiment with morning vs. night.

Aim for daily writing. Even 100 words keeps the story alive in your subconscious.

Use the 5‑minute rule. Sit down for five minutes. Often you’ll keep going.

Track your word count. Use a spreadsheet to see progress and gamify it.

3. Tools for Momentum
Start each session with a writer’s brief: bullet points of what you’ll write today.

End before you exhaust ideas: leave a sentence unfinished so you know where to start tomorrow.

Use placeholders for names or details you don’t know yet (e.g., [Name of merchant]).

Write at full intensity. Fast writing often produces more natural prose. You can polish later.

4. When You Get Stuck
Re‑outline. Your subconscious may be telling you something’s wrong.

Workshop with other writers. Explaining the problem often solves it.

Ask: “Why will this scene be somebody’s favorite?” Inject something you love.

Reconnect with your inspirations. Re‑watch/read what made you love fantasy.

V. Phase Five: Revision and Editing
1. Let the Draft Rest
After finishing the first draft, set it aside for a few weeks. Work on something else (a short story, a side project).

2. Read and Take Notes (Big Picture)
Print or transfer to e‑reader to gain objectivity.

Pretend you’re editing someone else’s story. Take notes on:

Structure: Are the nine points hitting?

Character arcs: Does the protagonist change believably?

Worldbuilding: Is anything confusing?

Pacing: Any soggy middle?

Each chapter: What works, what doesn’t?

3. Write the Second Draft (Structural Fixes)
Focus on big‑picture changes: adding or removing scenes, rearranging chapters, strengthening character arcs, cutting unnecessary characters, deepening themes.

Your likely structural areas: Make sure Frostfang has proper setup and payoff; ensure the Champion’s Gauntlet feels like a true midpoint; ensure his death is a culmination, not an afterthought.

4. Third Draft: Specific Editing Passes
Character pass: Go through and deepen one character at a time.

Dialogue pass: Make every voice distinctive. Shorten dialogue—it almost always improves.

Hook pass: Ensure each chapter starts and ends with something that pulls the reader forward.

Foreshadowing pass: If you added a twist later, go back and seed it earlier.

Setting pass: Add sensory details, weather, and interesting locations to avoid “white room” syndrome.

5. Get Feedback from Early Readers
When: After the third draft, when bones are solid but there’s still room to improve.

Who: Trusted readers who love fantasy and will give honest feedback.

What to ask: (Mary Robinette Kowal’s questions)

What’s great about the story? (Don’t accidentally cut it.)

What’s boring? (Cut or change.)

What confuses you? (Clarify.)

What don’t you believe? (Fix inconsistencies.)

Don’t ask for solutions (unless they’re experienced editors); ask for emotional experience.

6. Fourth Draft: Incorporate Feedback
Look for patterns: if multiple readers point out the same problem, fix it.

You don’t have to accept every note. But if the same issue comes up repeatedly, address it.

7. Professional Editing (Optional but Recommended)
Developmental editing (big picture) is most valuable for early drafts.

Line editing and copy editing come later.

Hiring an editor is an investment in your learning—you’ll carry those lessons to future books.

8. Final Polishing
Read aloud or use Word’s Read Aloud feature to catch awkward sentences.

Use ProWritingAid or similar to check for overused words, passive voice, sentence variation.

Read backwards to focus on individual sentences.

Change font or format to see the text with fresh eyes.

9. Know When to Stop
Art is never finished, only abandoned. When you feel diminishing returns—you’re making small tweaks but not improving the story—it’s time to let it go.

Then decide: pursue publication, or start the next book.

VI. Special Considerations for Fantasy
1. Magic System
Your system is hard: physics‑based, with clear rules and costs. This fits Sanderson’s First Law: the reader understands what’s possible.

Tip: Introduce the system gradually through scenes, not info‑dumps. Show the chain’s abilities in action, not all at once.

2. Worldbuilding
You’ve built six cultures with distinct magic, combat, and politics. Avoid infodumps—reveal worldbuilding through character experience.

The fourth party (beast‑kin, etc.) should be shown as complex societies, not just threats.

3. Avoiding Common Fantasy Pitfalls
Don’t beat the antagonist early: You avoided this.

Don’t make races inherently evil: You’ve subverted this.

Don’t let the protagonist become overpowered: His limits and costs keep him grounded.

VII. A Practical Timeline for Your Story
Given your detailed outline, you could aim for:

Months 1–2: Write childhood scenes and Frostfang chapter.

Months 3–4: Write Academy years (competitions, friendships, Varro rivalry, Champion’s Gauntlet).

Months 5–6: Write Adventuring years (freelance missions, meeting Renard, border war escalation).

Month 7: Write final stand and death.

Month 8: Write epilogue and any missing scenes.

Months 9–12: Revise (rest, big‑picture edits, feedback, polishing).

This is a rough guide; adjust to your pace.

VIII. Final Encouragement
You have built a world that is both expansive and coherent, and a protagonist whose “unspecial” nature is a deliberate and powerful statement. The writing advice from the videos confirms you’re on the right track. Now the only thing left is to write.

Remember:

The first draft only needs to exist.

Action creates motivation.

Finish a crappy draft—it’s easier to fix than a blank page.

You will learn more from finishing than from stopping halfway.

You have all the tools. Now go write.

If you’d like, I can help you break down the first section into a scene‑by‑scene outline, or provide a template for tracking your word count and daily progress. Just let me know.
